title: The cave of Hira
hookLine: near forty, he climbs to a small cave on a mountain above Mecca to think and pray alone

lines: A STEEP MOUNTAIN, A TINY CAVE.
cards: He has a good life now: a loving wife, children, a solid business, a name everyone trusts. Tradition says he's nearing forty. And something keeps pulling him out of town.
Outside Mecca there's a steep, rocky mountain. Near the top, tucked between boulders, is a cave. Tiny: room to sit, maybe to lie down, not much more.
That's where he starts going. Alone, carrying food and water up the mountain, staying days and nights at a time. Not to escape his family; he keeps coming back to them.
But to be somewhere quiet enough to think.

teach.h: JABAL AN-NUR, THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.
teach.b: The cave is called Hira. The mountain is known today as Jabal an-Nur, the Mountain of Light. The account comes down in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah.
Before revelation came, she says, he began to have dreams that came true, clear as the break of dawn.

teach.h: SOLITUDE WAS MADE DEAR TO HIM.
teach.b: Then, in her words as they've come down, solitude was made dear to him. He would worship in the cave of Hira for many nights, come back to Khadijah for more provisions, and go again.
The hadith's word for it is tahannuth, and it explains the word itself: worship, night after night, a kind of spiritual retreat. What exactly he prayed, and how, the sources don't say.
They tell us where, and for how long, and that he kept going back. Ibn Ishaq adds that he spent a month there every year, that the month was Ramadan, and that he fed the poor who came to him.
Remember the city he was pulling away from: the valley of idols and caravans from day seventy-eight. Up there, none of it.

Wind, rock, stars, and the city small below. People still climb to Hira today: a hard climb, rough steps cut into the mountain, and at the top a narrow gap in the rocks. It isn't part of any required ritual.
People go because he went, and because everything that comes next in his life, and in the life of Islam, starts in that small, quiet place.

how: Some Muslims keep a spiritual retreat, i'tikaf, staying in the mosque in the last ten nights of Ramadan; some pilgrims to Mecca climb Jabal an-Nur to see the cave of Hira, though it is not part of the rites.

o: the cave above Mecca where he went to pray
the month he spent alone every year
the mountain path pilgrims climb at Hajj

games.q: what's inside the cave — tap the pairs.

s: the sources record exactly how he prayed in the cave
they say where and for how long, not the words or the form.
visiting Hira is a required part of the pilgrimage
it isn't part of the rites; people climb because he went.
before revelation, he had dreams that came true like the break of dawn

games.q: you have a good life, a loving wife and a trusted name. something keeps pulling you toward quiet. what do you do?
o: climb to a cave and pray there alone, again and again.
games.why: solitude was made dear to him: he went to Hira for many nights, came home for provisions, and went back (Bukhari).

practice: If you can, go a few steps higher or further away, another room, a stairwell, a parked car, the far corner of a park, and sit for two minutes where nobody needs you.
Let the noise of the day get small below you, the way Mecca did from the mountain; you don't need to think of anything holy. If you pray, you can simply sit with Allah, without asking for anything.

wordCard.voice: Hira, the cave on the Mountain of Light above Mecca, where he went to be alone and pray, night after night.

orig.note: Arabic: Hira, the cave on Jabal an-Nur.

carryVoice: Your line: go up to the quiet. Tomorrow, the night everything changes. Day eighty-five, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (true dreams; solitude made dear; tahannuth in Hira)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (a month each year in Hira, in Ramadan; feeding the poor)
